description: Passionnés de science, de technologie et de jeux vidéo, nous participons au NASA Space Apps Challenge avec l’ambition de relever un défi de conception et de création de jeux (Défi 13). Nous souhaitons explorer de nouvelles idées, développer et transformer des concepts scientifiques en une expérience ludique, interactive et accessible.
summary:
Space Heroes is a browser game about the work that happens before a science mission ever flies. The player takes one seat on a small team, states the science question, and designs a spacecraft against six limits that move together: budget, mass, power, data, communications, and time. The launch that follows is not a painted sky. It plays a trajectory propagated in NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool. The debrief then places the result next to a real NASA mission.
The project answers the Design and Develop Science Missions challenge by making the design trade playable. A Concept Maturity Level gate has to be green before the team may leave a phase. Parts come from real classes: propulsion, structure, power, communications, and instrument. Three tests stand between the workshop and the pad. Eight missions are playable, from a 4 kg low-Earth CubeSat to the Moon, Mars, a Sun-Earth L1 halo, a polar orbit, a high orbit, and geostationary orbit. One player can fly alone. Four players on the same network can share the gauges.
What matters is that a student, or a judge, can finish a mission on a laptop without installing a flight-dynamics tool, and can still see where each figure came from. The orbits were computed in GMAT R2026a and stored for the game to display. The browser does not invent a new lunar capture, a new Mars window, or a new station contact. Where the project uses an assumption, as with the four station-keeping maneuvers a year at L1, the screen says so.
details:
The path of a mission

Space Heroes is a progressive web app. One generic engine reads each mission from data. A mission always follows the same path: headquarters, role, briefing, workshop, three tests, launch, operations, and debrief.

At headquarters the player sees eight missions. In Campaign, chapter 1 is open and each following chapter opens when the previous one has a debrief score. Discovery mode opens all eight. The solar-system map uses the same lock. It opens as a schematic that is not to scale. One button, Orrery, replaces that line with moving orbits. Schematic brings the line back.

The player picks one of four seats: Mission Director, Vehicle Engineer, Systems Engineer, or Science Lead. Alone, ASTRA covers the other three. She speaks lines written for each step. The briefing asks for the science goal, what makes the mission specific, the window, the budget class, and a first sketch. Later gates use a 20-line checklist. A phase opens when 80 percent of the required checks are green.

Workshop, tests, launch

The workshop selects one component in each of five families. Twelve points set the balance of the chosen part. Six resources move together. On the low-Earth chapter, twelve mission weeks lose part of the 350 kilometers between the starting altitude margin and a 200 kilometer circular orbit. That loss is the semi-major-axis drop propagated for 84 days, on four CubeSat faces: 0.0100, 0.01702, 0.0227, and 0.03405 square meters. At 1.33 kilograms those faces lose 43.1, 65.5, 85.5, and 137.6 kilometers. The 3U face at 1.33 kilograms reaches 200 kilometers on day 114.8. Outside 1.33 to 4 kilograms the loss is extended as one over mass, and the workshop says so.

Three tests follow: vibration, thermal isolation, and electrical compatibility. If the gate blocks the exit, the team can return to the workshop. The cost already charged is replaced, not added again.

Launch plays the stored trajectory in Three.js. The rocket on screen is deliberately larger than scale. The altitude in the legend is the real one from the chapter table. After insertion, three buttons frame the orbit already computed: Overview, Satellite, and Moon. Moon appears only on the lunar transfer.

Operations, debrief, and a table of four

Operations run a ground contact, then deploy communications, power, and the instrument, in that order. The debrief scores the mission out of 100, compares it with a real NASA mission, and exports a PDF.

A party of four uses a separate Node server. The server owns the six gauges and the veto reserve. Voice, if allowed, travels from browser to browser. There is no TURN server and no public host. The solo game never needs the server.

Tools and purpose

The page is Vite 5, JavaScript modules, and Three.js 0.160. Trajectories were propagated with GMAT R2026a and copied into JSON. The page does not call GMAT. The optional orrery uses the JPL Keplerian elements for 1800–2050, with the published rotation. The Moon starts at the new moon of 8 January 2008.4849 and advances by the sidereal month of 27.32166 days.

The goal is to teach the trades of a science mission with figures that can be checked, to label a hypothesis as a hypothesis, and to let a player finish without installing a flight-dynamics tool.
